content: Periodinanes are chemical compounds that contain hypervalent iodine atoms. Hypervalency refers to the presence of more than eight electrons in the valence shell of the iodine atom, which exceeds the octet rule. When iodine is bonded to a monodentate electronegative ligand, such as chlorine, it can exist in two oxidation states: +3 (iodine(III), also called λ3-iodanes) or +5 (iodine(V), also called λ5-iodanes). Iodine itself has seven valence electrons, but in λ3-iodanes, three additional electrons are donated by the ligands, resulting in a total of ten valence electrons (a decet structure). In λ5-iodanes, the ligands donate enough electrons to create a twelve-electron (dodecet) structure. In contrast, non-hypervalent iodine compounds, such as iodobenzene, adhere to the octet rule with eight valence electrons. To form hypervalent iodine compounds, iodine undergoes oxidation, losing three or five electrons. The ligands then donate electron pairs to form coordinate covalent bonds, contributing six or ten electrons back to the iodine atom. This bonding is described using the L-I-N notation, where L represents the number of electrons donated by the ligands, and N represents the number of ligands. The concept of hypervalent iodine was first introduced by J.J. Musher in 1969. To explain the excess electrons in hypervalent compounds, the three-center, four-electron bond model was proposed, analogous to the three-center, two-electron bond seen in electron-deficient compounds. In iodine(III) compounds, one such bond exists, while iodine(V) compounds contain two of these bonds. The first hypervalent iodine compound, dichloroiodobenzene (C6H5Cl2I), was synthesized in 1886 by the German chemist C. Willgerodt by passing chlorine gas through iodobenzene dissolved in chloroform. λ3-Iodanes, such as diarylchloroiodanes, exhibit a pseudotrigonal bipyramidal geometry. In these compounds, the apical positions are occupied by a phenyl group and a chlorine atom, while the equatorial positions are occupied by another phenyl group and two lone pairs of electrons. λ5-Iodanes, such as the Dess-Martin periodinane, have a square pyramidal geometry, with four heteroatoms in the basal positions and a phenyl group at the apical position. Classical organic synthesis methods exist for preparing hypervalent iodine compounds. For example, iodosobenzene diacetate can be synthesized from peracetic acid and acetic acid. A related compound, phenyliodine bis(trifluoroacetate) (PIFA), is derived from trifluoroacetic acid. Iodosobenzene diacetate can be hydrolyzed with water to produce iodoxybenzene (C6H5O2I), also known as iodylbenzene, which is a known oxidizing agent. This compound was first prepared by Willgerodt through the disproportionation of iodosylbenzene under steam distillation, yielding iodylbenzene and iodobenzene. Alternatively, iodosobenzene diacetate can be hydrolyzed with sodium hydroxide to produce iodosylbenzene, which is actually a polymer with the molecular formula (C6H5OI)n. Iodosylbenzene is widely used in organic oxidation reactions. The Dess-Martin periodinane, developed in 1983, is another powerful oxidizing agent. It is an improvement over the IBX acid, which was first synthesized in 1893. IBX acid is prepared from 2-iodobenzoic acid, potassium bromate, and sulfuric acid. However, IBX acid is insoluble in most solvents, whereas the Dess-Martin reagent, prepared by reacting IBX acid with acetic anhydride, is highly soluble. The oxidation mechanism of these reagents typically involves a ligand exchange reaction followed by reductive elimination. The primary application of hypervalent iodine compounds is as oxidizing agents, often replacing toxic heavy-metal-based reagents. Current research is exploring their use in forming carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bonds. For example, in one study, an intramolecular C-N coupling reaction was achieved using a catalytic amount of aryliodide in trifluoroethanol. In this reaction, the periodinane intermediate (referred to as intermediate A) is formed by oxidizing the aryliodide with mCPBA, a sacrificial oxidant. This intermediate then converts a hydroxylamine group into a nitrenium ion (intermediate B), which acts as an electrophile. The nitrenium ion undergoes ipso addition to an aromatic ring, resulting in the formation of a lactam containing an enone functional group.
